title: What Is Intelligent Automation? Components, Examples, and How It Differs From RPA
summary: Intelligent automation combines AI, RPA and process management. Learn its parts, real portal examples, how it differs from RPA, and how to start.
body_markdown:
Intelligent automation (IA) is the use of artificial intelligence together with process automation tools, mainly robotic process automation (RPA) and business process management (BPM), to run business processes that involve reading, deciding and acting.[IBM defines it](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/intelligent-automation?ref=skyvern.com) as the combination of AI, BPM and RPA "to streamline and scale decision-making across organizations." The same idea also goes by intelligent process automation (IPA) and cognitive automation.


The AI part is what separates it from plain automation. An RPA bot repeats steps someone recorded. Intelligent automation adds software that can read a document, sort a request or choose the next step when the input changes. That lets work that used to need a person at every step run from start to finish, with people stepping in for the cases that need them.


This guide covers intelligent automation in business operations: back-office work such as claims, invoices, credential checks and portal tasks. It leaves out factory robotics, which some definitions also include.


We build Skyvern, an AI browser automation platform that operations teams use for portal work on websites that have no API. The examples in this guide come from those jobs.


## What makes a process intelligent automation


A process counts as intelligent automation when software handles steps that need judgment, as well as the steps that follow fixed rules. In practice, that shows up as four characteristics:


- **It works with unstructured inputs.** Emails, PDFs, scanned forms and web pages, as well as the structured data in spreadsheets and databases. IBM describes the AI component as analyzing both kinds of data.
- **It makes or proposes decisions inside the process.** Typical decisions are classifying a document, extracting the right fields, matching records or choosing where a case goes next.
- **It connects steps across systems.** One automation can read an email, update a record in one system and submit a form in another.
- **It hands uncertain cases to a person.** A well-built process routes exceptions to someone on the team instead of guessing.


## The components of intelligent automation


Intelligent automation combines three core functions: interpreting information, managing a process and carrying out tasks. AI, business process management and RPA handle those jobs. Document processing and AI agents help when the work involves documents or steps that can change.


### Artificial intelligence: interpreting information


AI turns incoming information into something a workflow can act on. It can classify a customer request, match records or read an email to identify what someone needs. The workflow uses that result to decide what happens next.


For example, AI can identify an invoice dispute in an email and route it to the billing team.


### Intelligent document processing: extracting document data


Intelligent document processing (IDP) takes information from documents and puts it into usable fields. It identifies the document type, extracts values and checks them against validation rules.


For an invoice, those fields might include the supplier, invoice number, amount and due date. The workflow can then match them against a purchase order, send discrepancies for review and pass approved data to the accounting system.


### Business process management: coordinating the work


Business process management (BPM) defines how work moves from start to finish. It establishes the steps, their order and who is responsible for each one.


Workflow software puts that process into operation: routing approvals, tracking progress and handling exceptions. In an invoice process, it determines who must approve the payment and what happens if the amounts do not match.


### Robotic process automation: executing repeatable tasks


RPA performs defined, repeatable actions in software. A bot can enter data, fill in forms, download files and move information between systems.


It works best when the steps and interfaces are predictable. For example, a bot can take approved invoice data and enter it into an accounting application that has no suitable API.


### AI agents: choosing the next action


AI agents work toward a goal and choose their next action based on what they find. This helps when the route through a task varies.


An agent checking insurance coverage might sign in to a payer portal, find the patient, open the relevant plan and retrieve coverage details. Its next step depends on the page and information in front of it. The surrounding workflow defines its access, required checks and when to involve a person.


### How the parts work together


A purchase order can move from an email attachment into an order-management system without someone retyping it. Here’s a typical workflow:


1. **The order arrives.** A customer emails a purchase order as a PDF.
2. **Document AI extracts the details.** It identifies the document and pulls out the customer name, products, quantities and delivery address.
3. **Business rules check the data.** The system checks for missing fields, unknown product codes and duplicate orders. The workflow sends problems to a person for review and routes orders that need approval to the right team.
4. **RPA enters the approved order.** A bot creates the order in the company’s software when no suitable API is available.
5. **The workflow records the result.** It saves the order number, updates the case status and notifies the fulfillment team.


Document AI reads the input, business rules check it, workflow software coordinates the handoffs, and RPA handles the data entry. People handle exceptions and required approvals.


Different tools own interpretation, routing and execution.


## Intelligent automation vs RPA vs hyperautomation vs agentic automation


These four terms overlap because they share tools. They differ in scope and in who decides the next step.


Term What it is Scope Who decides the next step


RPA Software bots that repeat rule-based steps Single repetitive tasks The recorded script


Intelligent automation (IPA) AI combined with BPM and RPA Tasks that need reading or judgment, often linked into a process Rules and AI models, with people for exceptions


Hyperautomation Automating everything an organization can automate Every eligible process, plus the coordination between tools and people An orchestration layer


Agentic automation AI agents working toward a goal Goal-level work across steps and systems The agent, within limits the team sets


**RPA vs intelligent automation.** RPA executes predefined steps. Intelligent automation adds the ability to interpret information and make decisions. An RPA bot can enter invoice fields into an accounting system. Intelligent automation can first extract those fields from a PDF, check them against a purchase order and send discrepancies for review. RPA handles the data entry; the broader workflow handles the document and the checks.


**Hyperautomation.** Hyperautomation is the strategy for expanding automation across a business. It involves finding processes worth automating, choosing suitable tools and connecting workflows across teams and systems. Intelligent automation might handle invoice processing. A hyperautomation program could connect that process with purchasing, inventory and payments, with shared controls and measures of performance.


**Agentic automation.**[Agentic automation](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/what-is-agentic-automation-ops-guide/) gives an AI agent a goal and lets it choose actions based on what happens during the task. For example, an agent checking insurance coverage can respond to different portal screens, locate the relevant plan and retrieve the required details. This suits work where the path varies between cases. The team defines the agent’s access, approval requirements and checks for successful completion.


## Intelligent automation examples


Here are five examples of intelligent automation based on what our clients automate with Skyvern. In each case, we handle repetitive work across websites so their teams spend less time entering data and chasing documents.


### Prior authorization on payer portals


Our healthcare clients use Skyvern to[submit prior authorization requests](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/automate-healthcare-prior-authorization-insurance-portals/) , upload supporting documents and check request status across payer portals. This reduces manual data entry and repeated follow-ups, giving staff more time to resolve requests that need their attention.


### Insurance eligibility checks


Our clients automate[insurance eligibility checks](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/automating-healthcare-insurance-eligibility-verification/) before patient visits. Skyvern retrieves coverage and benefits information across payer portals and returns it to the team. Staff can review the results without looking up every patient manually.


### Credential verification on the BACB registry


Behavioral health clients use Skyvern to[verify RBT and BCBA credentials](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/automating-rbt-bcba-credential-verification-behavioral-health/) against the BACB registry and record the results. We automate the repeated searches and status checks, helping onboarding teams spot discrepancies and maintain a record of each verification.


### Invoice downloads from vendor portals


Our finance clients use Skyvern to[collect invoices from vendor portals](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/how-to-automate-downloading-invoices-september-2025/) and deliver the files to cloud storage. This removes the monthly routine of signing into each account and downloading invoices individually, so the team can focus on reconciliation and payment.


### Quotes and documents on insurance carrier portals


Insurance agencies use Skyvern to[request quotes and retrieve documents across carrier portals](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/automate-insurance-carrier-portal-workflows/) . We automate entering client details and collecting files, reducing duplicate work so agents can spend more time comparing coverage and advising clients.


## How to start an intelligent automation project


Start with one process that runs often, has few judgment calls and produces a result you can check. Then expand. Here is a simple framework for a first project:


1. **Pick the process.** Good first candidates repeat many times a week, follow written steps and end with something easy to verify, like a downloaded file or an updated status. Our own advice is to make one recurring process dependable before you extend it to more request types or sites.
2. **Map where judgment happens.** List each step and mark which ones follow rules and which ones need a person. The second group becomes your review points.
3. **Write down the procedure.** A clear standard operating procedure (SOP) makes the automation easier to build and to check.
4. **Test on cases you've already handled.** Run the automation on last month's work and compare its output with what your team produced. For invoice downloads, that means checking the files against a month you already collected.
5. **Measure.** Track time per case and cases handled per person, before and after.
6. **Expand.** Add the next site, request type or team once the first process runs reliably.

## FAQ


### Is intelligent automation the same as intelligent process automation (IPA)?


Yes, in most usage. Both names describe the same combination of AI, business process management and RPA. Some sources also use hyperautomation as a synonym, while others treat it as the larger, organization-wide effort.


### Is AI the same as automation?


No. Automation runs steps that are defined in advance. AI interprets information and makes predictions or decisions, such as reading a scanned form or choosing which queue a request belongs in. Intelligent automation combines the two in one process.


### What is the main purpose of intelligent process automation?


Its purpose is to let processes that involve reading and judgment run from start to finish with less manual work.[IBM lists the benefits](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/intelligent-automation?ref=skyvern.com) as higher productivity, more consistent and accurate work, faster service for customers and more consistent compliance. For an ops team, that usually means handling more volume with the same people, who spend their time on the cases that need them.
